THE DAILY POST | Correction

Yesterday we reported that a leaking (漏水的) roof forced Green Lane residents (居民) to leave their flats. In fact, firefighters asked them to leave after smoke (烟) from a nearby warehouse (仓库) entered the building. The roof was damaged later, during the operation (行动). We apologise (道歉) for the error.

A pattern of my own

(11) ____ carefully I applied the dye (染料) afterwards, I could not control where it went. The unprotected cotton quickly (12) ____ the dye, leaving a green patch where the cloth was supposed to remain white.

I was ready to start again when our tutor asked me to turn the cloth around. From the other side, the patch looked rather like a second leaf. Instead of treating it as something to remove, she encouraged me to (13) ____ what was already there. She suggested (14) ____ a few smaller leaves around it, without copying the arrangement (排列) on the sample.

I tested the idea on paper before adding more wax. The extra leaves helped the unwanted patch (15) ____ in with the rest of the design. Gradually, I began to understand the (17) ____ between a thoughtful (经过思考的) design and a perfectly regular (规则的) one.

My cloth did not resemble (像) the sample I had chosen, but I no longer minded. I had arrived expecting a lesson in following instructions. What I took away was a lesson in (18) ____: when the original plan failed, I could respond to what was actually in front of me.

READING — PART 3

A different place on the team

1 When the starting team for our school volleyball tournament (锦标赛) was announced, I applauded with everyone else. Then I checked the list again, although I already knew my name was not there. I would travel with the squad (队伍) as a reserve (替补). Coach offered me a notebook and asked whether I could record useful observations (观察) during matches. I accepted before he finished speaking. If I could not be on court, I wanted a reason to feel that the afternoon still involved me. Privately, though, I hoped the notebook would soon be replaced by a chance to play.

2 At our next practice match, I filled three pages. I counted missed serves, marked where points were lost and underlined (画线标出) the same player’s name several times. Handing over the notebook, I expected Coach to be impressed by my attention (注意力). He read it, then asked what we should do differently. I pointed to the underlined name. “That tells me who you noticed,” he said. “What does it tell that player to try?” My figures (数据) were not wrong, but they offered a list of disappointments (失误) rather than a useful next step.

3 I spoke to the player, Mira, afterwards. I had assumed (以为) she was slow to react because she looked uncertain (不确定的) whenever the ball came towards her. She explained that she could often reach it, but hesitated (犹豫) when another teammate moved towards the same space. In my notes, I had recorded only the person closest to the ball when it landed. Mira asked to see the page. I nearly closed the book, embarrassed (尴尬的) by how confidently I had judged something I had not understood. Instead, I let her read it, and we worked out what I should watch during the next practice.

4 My second set of notes contained fewer totals and more questions. Did two players call for the same ball? Could the quieter player be heard from the back of the court? I also marked occasions (情况) when their communication worked. That mattered: without those examples, I might have described an occasional (偶尔的) problem as a permanent (长期的) weakness. Coach used two of our observations in training, but left another aside. I was disappointed until he explained that solving every problem at once would leave the team trying to remember too much.

READING — PART 3

A different place on the team — Continued

5 During the tournament, the notebook proved less tidy (整齐的) than it had at practice. Opponents (对手) changed their positions, the hall became noisy and I missed several things while writing. At one break, I thought our team should move a player forward. Coach agreed that this might stop the short shots troubling us, but asked what space it would leave behind. He chose a smaller adjustment (调整). I could see the problem clearly from my seat; I had not seen the cost (代价) of the solution quite as clearly.

6 We won that match narrowly. On the bus home, a teammate joked that my notebook must contain the secret of our success. I laughed but did not pass it around. Mira had trusted (信任) me with a conversation, not given me material for the whole bus to discuss. Besides, our opponents had made mistakes too, and no set of notes could explain every point. I wrote a short summary (总结) of the communication patterns for Coach, leaving out the personal comments that had helped me understand them.

7 I am still a reserve, and I still watch Coach whenever he considers a substitution (换人). Discovering a useful job beside the court has not removed my wish to play. Yet I no longer think the only meaningful contribution (贡献) is the one everyone can see on the scoreboard (记分板). The notebook has not made me an expert. It has made me slower to decide what I know, and rather better at asking what I have missed.

Watching without the sound

Our class had made a short comedy (喜剧) about an unexpected visitor. Before the school film festival, we wanted to add captions (字幕) so that the story could be followed without sound. I typed every spoken word and placed the text below the picture. During a trial (试播), however, viewers kept pausing (暂停) the film to read. (27) ____ We needed to reduce the amount on screen without losing anything important.

Some cuts were easy: repeated greetings (问候语) did not add much. Others changed the story. In one scene, a character promised to arrive “before lunch”, but I shortened the line to “I’ll come”. Later, her friends complained (抱怨) that she was late. (28) ____ We restored the time reference (信息) and found less important words to remove elsewhere.

Another scene showed two people listening while someone spoke from the next room. We could recognise (辨认) the voice because we knew the cast, but the viewers could not. (29) ____ Adding the speaker’s name before that line solved the problem without requiring us to change the picture.

Not every important sound was speech. A loud crash (撞击声) interrupted a conversation, making both characters jump. The visitor had dropped a box, but the audience was not supposed to learn that yet. (30) ____ We used “[a crash outside]”, leaving the explanation to the following scene. Describing what had happened too precisely (精确地) would have spoiled (破坏) the surprise.

Timing (时机) needed attention as well. When I placed a question and its reply on screen together, viewers read both before either character had finished speaking. (31) ____ Separating the two captions brought back the brief uncertainty (不确定感) that made the exchange funny. It also gave viewers time to notice the questioning character’s expression (表情).

For the last test, we invited students who had never seen the film. They watched with the sound off and told us where the story stopped making sense. (32) ____ Their comments led to two final changes. We had spent so long making the film that we had forgotten what a new viewer did not already know.

READING — PART 5

Behind the finished project

A — Amira
Our exhibition posters had attracted (吸引) hundreds of online reactions (反应), so I expected a crowd. Only a few visitors came. I later asked people who had liked the post and learnt that most had never noticed the date. We kept the artwork but placed the practical details (细节) where they could be read at a glance (一眼就看懂). For the next event, I counted bookings (预约) rather than reactions. A smaller figure could tell us more.
B — Brandon
I normally designed the posters while others handled visitors. When our exhibition guide (讲解员) became ill, I reluctantly took her place. I thought I would need to memorise (记住) every fact. Instead, I carried a short list and asked visitors which objects interested them. Their questions kept the conversation moving. I still enjoy designing, but I no longer volunteer (主动承担) for it simply to avoid meeting people.
C — Chitra
Our group wanted a professionally printed exhibition catalogue (目录册). After calculating the cost (成本), we realised that printing fewer copies would still use most of our budget (预算). We made simple folded leaflets (传单) instead, then asked the same writer to check every description. The leaflets lacked glossy (光面的) pages, but retained the carefully researched information. It was the finish we could afford to change, rather than the accuracy (准确性).

READING — PART 5

Behind the finished project — Continued

D — Danish
The first exhibition rota (轮值表) was very efficient (高效的): I gave each person the job they already did best. Everyone finished quickly, but two members said they had joined to try something unfamiliar (不熟悉的). We paired experienced members with beginners (初学者) and allowed extra time. I still kept a rota; it now balanced (平衡) a smooth event with a chance for people to develop. Doing everything fastest was no longer our only aim.
E — Elisa
I wanted to replace our quiet music exhibition with something more modern. Before choosing a new theme (主题), we invited a few teenagers to try the existing one. They stayed much longer when they could press buttons and hear short recordings (录音). We kept the old photographs and stories, but added headphones (耳机) beside them. What had seemed like a problem with the subject was really about how visitors could explore (探索) it.
F — Fahmi
Our exhibition interviews sounded natural, but editing (剪辑) them took far longer than expected. Important details were scattered (分散) across the recordings, and we kept searching for the same moment. We began writing timestamps (时间戳) beside brief notes while recording each new interview. This did not shorten the conversations or decide what would appear in the final display. It simply made the recorded material easier to find afterwards.
